data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference smuggles induction back in because any justification for acting on the better-corroborated theory implicitly assumes the future will resemble the past (the Principle of Uniformity). To say 'Theory A worked before, so I will use it now' is an inductive leap. Even if labeled 'pragmatic,' the expectation that a theory which survived severe tests will continue to yield successful predictions or technological applications relies on the very inductive habit Popper sought to excise from the logic of science.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If one accepts Hume's skepticism fully and abandons the expectation of future success, the preference becomes irrational.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If 'pragmatic success' is redefined strictly as 'current non-falsification' without reference to future application.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the agent explicitly disavows any expectation of future predictive success.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The psychological and practical act of 'preference' creates a bridge between past performance and future utility. This bridge is structurally identical to induction: P(Theories surviving tests T have been useful) -> P(This theory surviving T will be useful). Popper's distinction between 'logical probability' and 'pragmatic preference' is a semantic shield that fails to block the underlying epistemic commitment to the stability of natural laws required to make the preference rational.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
